text: The $500,000 joint limit on tax-free gain from selling a main home has not changed since it took effect in May 1997; in August 2026 prices that 1997 limit would be about $1,046,000.
A couple who bought in 2000 crosses the limit when their gain (sale price minus purchase price and improvements) exceeds $500,000.

If their home rose in value like its metro's price index from 2000 to 2026 Q2, that happens once the 2000 purchase price was above about $114,700 in Miami, $151,500 in Los Angeles, $164,500 in San Diego, $179,200 in Phoenix, $180,000 in Seattle, $212,200 in New York, $215,600 in Dallas, $226,400 in Boston, $227,700 in Denver, $254,400 in San Jose, $259,000 in San Francisco and $373,400 in Chicago (national index: $243,500; for a single seller with the $250,000 limit: $121,700).
In 11 of these 12 metros the threshold is under $300,000 and in 5 it is under $200,000.
Gain above the limit is taxed as a long-term capital gain on a sale, while heirs who inherit the home take a basis equal to its value at death.

text: Long-time owners widely assume a married couple's home sale is tax-free because '$500,000 is more than our profit', and that the limit is something only expensive coastal homes ever reach.

In 11 of the 12 metros a 2000 purchase price under $300,000 is already enough for an index-typical gain to exceed the limit, including non-coastal metros such as Phoenix and Dallas, so the tax on the excess gain can become a real input in a sell-now-versus-keep decision that owners assume is tax-free.
A viewer can check the threshold for their metro against their own purchase price plus improvements.

Bought Your Home in 2000? The $500,000 Tax-Free Limit Test
Married homeowners who bought their house in 2000 and are now weighing a sale to downsize.
Sell the house we bought in 2000 now, or keep it, given the $500,000 tax-free limit on home-sale gains?
We measure, metro by metro, how far typical home-price growth since 2000 has pushed sellers' gains against a limit that never moved with inflation.
